items.title: Old threads open their newest replies much faster
items.summary: The workspace's database now files replies by thread and in order. The server can jump straight to the newest replies of an old thread.
items.before: To show the newest replies of an old thread, the server could read through the channel's newer, unrelated messages and sort them before it found the replies it wanted.
items.after: The server goes straight to that thread's replies, already in order. The old way of finding replies was replaced, not kept beside the new one.
items.mechanism: The composite index matches both the equality filter and message-order range used by thread pages and has-more probes.

technical.title: Seek directly through thread history
technical.summary: Schema v28 replaces the old single-column reply index with (thread_root_id, id), speeding sparse old-thread tail reads.
technical.before: A thread tail without a cursor could scan a channel's unrelated newer messages and sort before finding the requested replies.
technical.after: The SQLite plan seeks the requested thread's ordered range directly; the old index is replaced rather than retained alongside a duplicate.
limits: Historical Linux Xeon/Node 24.21 fixture with 30 warm HTTP samples; not a current installation capacity claim.
Cursor-bounded pages were already fast and showed no comparable gain. Extra index space/build/write cost is part of the decision.

items.title: Unrelated changes no longer redraw every message
items.summary: Each message on screen now watches only the people and channels it shows, plus your own identity and role. It no longer watches the whole list of people and channels.
items.before: When someone unrelated edited their profile, someone joined another channel, or you changed your own status, the app redrew all 300 loaded messages.
items.after: Unrelated changes redraw no messages. Renaming a person redraws only the messages that show that person. Permission changes still update the buttons they affect.
items.mechanism: Stable derived entity selectors preserve object references while unchanged maps/entries remain semantically equal.

technical.title: Render only rows whose displayed entities changed
technical.summary: Message rows subscribe to the author, mentioned/reacting users, referenced channels and primitive self identity/role instead of entire maps.
technical.before: An unrelated user's profile edit, other-channel membership or own status change rendered all 300 loaded rows.
technical.after: Unrelated changes render zero rows; renaming an author updates only rows that show that author, while permission changes still update the affected controls.

Selectors add small per-event work and the change added about 1 kB to that historical entry.

items.title: Mention counts and Activity load much faster
items.summary: The server now keeps a list of who each message mentions. It no longer rereads every message in every channel to count each person's mentions.
items.before: Each recount reread the text of messages in every channel the person had joined. A message that mentioned everyone in a channel repeated that work for every member.
items.after: Unread counts and the Activity view start from the messages that mention the person directly or mention everyone. Then the usual rules for what is read in channels and threads apply.
items.mechanism: Store updates message_mentions transactionally on create/edit/delete; retention cascades its rows. The migration parses existing text under the same mention rules.

technical.title: Start unread mention work from the mentions index
technical.summary: Schema v31 materializes message-to-recipient mention membership instead of scanning every channel message for each account's count.
technical.before: Every recount rechecked message text across joined channels; a room-wide mention repeated that work for every member.
technical.after: Counts and Activity start from the account's direct or room-wide mention candidates, then apply the shared channel/thread read rule.
limits: Historical seeded measurements; text scanning/index maintenance raises send work and slightly increases database size.
Thread unread semantics remain authoritative; older clients may not understand later unreadHold additions.

items.title: Connecting to a big workspace is about four times faster
items.summary: When the app connects, the server sends a starting picture of the workspace. Two parts of building it took longer the more people a workspace had, and both are now cheaper.
items.before: To list channels, the server asked about each channel's managers and members one channel at a time, and finding managers meant looking through ordinary members too. To show who is online, it loaded every person just to mark them offline.
items.after: The server keeps a short list of channel managers and gathers channel details in two shared lookups. The online list names only the people who are online.
items.mechanism: Only is_manager=1 membership rows enter the new index. Missing presence already means offline in the client, and snapshots replace the map rather than merge stale online entries.

limits: Measured in the past on one test computer. In big workspaces, the full list of people is still most of what is sent on connect.
Sending less at sign-in, or loading the People list a page at a time, would need a change to the shared rules, not just a faster lookup.

technical.title: Build snapshots with batched managers and sparse presence
technical.summary: Schema v34 and batched list reads remove two handshake costs that scaled with the account/member count.
technical.before: The channel list made one manager/member query per channel; manager lookups scanned ordinary members. Presence reloaded all users to mark them offline.
technical.after: A partial manager index and two shared reads build visible channel metadata; the presence map names only online accounts.
limits: Historical workload and host; the complete users list still dominates large snapshots.
Lean account bootstrap/paged People would require a further protocol decision, not just this query optimization.

items.title: Searching common words and file names is faster
items.summary: The server now picks a different way to search depending on the words. It shows exactly the same results and still respects who can see what.
items.before: Searching for a common word meant gathering and sorting every matching message just to show one page. Searches for rarer words checked over and over whether each file name could match.
items.after: For a common word, the server looks through the newest messages first, within a limited range, and falls back to a full search when needed. For rarer words, it gathers text matches and file name matches once and then combines them.
items.mechanism: A match count capped at 5,001 selects the path. Terms over the 5,000 threshold keep a 20,000-message window; the F13 sparse branch uses full-text rows UNION ALL file-message rows, then shared hydration/filtering.

limits: The two speed comparisons were measured on different past versions of the code. Do not add their gains together.

Searches for rare words, for words mostly found in channels you cannot see, or inside one channel can take slightly longer because of an extra first count. Two other approaches were tried and rejected.
Faster lookups for searching by a rare author or by date were researched but not added. The speed figures only hold for the test workspaces that were measured.

technical.title: Keep common-word search bounded and sparse/name search selective
technical.summary: Two delivered search changes choose the appropriate query shape while preserving exact page content and access filters.
technical.before: A common word required resolving, joining and sorting every matching message for one page; filename eligibility was repeatedly evaluated in sparse queries.
technical.after: Common full-text terms use a newest-first scoped window with exact fallback; sparse terms combine bounded text matches and filename rowids once.
limits: The two comparisons use different historical revisions; their gains must not be added.
Rare/hidden/in-channel queries can pay small admission overhead. Blanket message-ID UNION and separate filename-statement experiments were rejected.
No rare-author/date index was rolled out from research candidates; benchmark promises are limited to tested fixtures.

items.title: Screens used once download only when opened
items.summary: The join, profile and friends screens now download only when someone opens them, like several other dialogs and panels already did.
items.before: People already signed in still downloaded the code for screens used once, like joining a workspace, even though they did not need it to show their chats.
items.after: Those screens download when opened. This freed up room under the 500 kilobyte limit on what the app downloads first.
items.mechanism: React lazy imports and Suspense boundaries split code while keeping the shared application route behavior and chunk-failure handling.

technical.title: Move first-use-only screens and dialogs out of the entry
technical.summary: Join, profile and friends screens join other deferred dialogs/panels as lazy modules.
technical.before: Returning signed-in readers downloaded code for first-use screens that they did not need during initial chat rendering.
technical.after: Those modules load on use, restoring measured historical headroom under the 500 kB entry guard.

Later features consume the restored headroom: the N01–N12 build recorded web 496,783 and desktop 499,463 bytes against 500,000.

items.title: Threads and message links are not rebuilt for no reason
items.summary: The threads kept in the app's copy of the workspace, and the address used to build links to messages, are no longer rebuilt when something unrelated changes.
items.before: A new message in some other channel could make the app rebuild every thread it had kept. When the desktop app hosts the server, each change in how many people are connected or in backup status could rebuild the address used for message links, so every message on screen redrew.
items.after: Only the threads and pages a new message belongs to are rebuilt. The address for message links changes only when a link would actually change.
items.mechanism: Route live events by message/root ownership; derive provider values from address-relevant fields rather than the entire hosting snapshot.
limits: Tests confirm that unchanged parts are left alone. The earlier speed measurement was not repeated in the later review.
While older messages are still loading, live updates are still held back and applied in order, as before.

technical.title: Preserve unchanged thread and link-context references
technical.summary: Client cache and hosting/link context updates avoid rebuilding unrelated visible content.
technical.before: An unrelated channel message could slice/replace every cached thread, and a connected-count/backup-status update could invalidate shared message-link context.
technical.after: Only relevant threads/pages and semantically changed link fields receive new references.
limits: Correct reference preservation is covered; the historical Profiler comparison was not rerun in the later follow-up review.
In-flight history still buffers ordered events under the snapshot watermark rules.

items.title: Fewer duplicate loads, and Activity stops going blank
items.summary: When the app asks for the same piece of history twice, both requests now share one download. A burst of new mentions leads to only a couple of Activity refreshes.
items.before: Asking for the same page of history again started a second request and cancelled one of them. A burst of mentions made the Activity view go blank and reload again and again.
items.after: Matching requests for history get their answer from one download. Requests for a page the app no longer needs are cancelled. Activity keeps showing its list until the new one arrives.
items.mechanism: Each history run has AbortController plus request/window identity; CoalescedLoader debounces automatic changes for 250 ms and permits at most one follow-up load while active. Explicit filter/page/Refresh loads remain immediate.

metrics.label: Requests made for a burst of ten Activity changes
metrics.detail: Requests for the recorded ten-change Activity burst

limits: This counts requests and checks what stays on screen. It does not measure how much faster anything feels.
Requests for different pages, real network failures, catching up on live updates, message order and shutting the workspace down all behave as before.

technical.title: Share equivalent history requests and coalesce Activity refreshes
technical.summary: Equivalent tail/older/thread/newer loads share a transfer, and automatic Activity updates collapse into bounded work.
technical.before: Repeated equivalent paging started duplicate requests and aborted one; a mention burst repeatedly blanked/refetched Activity.
technical.after: Equivalent cursor/window callers settle from one request, replaced windows cancel, and Activity remains visible until the new answer arrives.
limits: This records request-count and visible-state controls, not an end-to-end latency benchmark.
Changed cursors/windows, real network failures, live replay, ordering and destruction retain their existing semantics.

items.title: Private replies from apps no longer pile up
items.summary: The app keeps a limited number of private replies to commands, with a cap on their total text. A reply that arrives again replaces its earlier copy.
items.before: In a long session, private replies to commands could pile up without limit, in number and in size, outside the normal message history.
items.after: The app keeps up to 20 of these replies per conversation and 100 overall, with a limit on their total text. A repeated reply replaces the earlier one instead of showing twice.
items.mechanism: Admission/eviction operates on the private-answer collection, preserving durable workspace messages and the active visible reply behavior.
limits: The recorded test result comes from one test setup. It is not the limit itself and does not guarantee how much memory the whole app uses.
Checking this with a screen reader and with real scrolling is still a separate task.

technical.title: Bound transient private app answers
technical.summary: Private command replies retained by the client have count and text budgets, with replacement by repeated IDs.
technical.before: Long sessions could accumulate arbitrarily many or large private answers outside bounded durable history.
technical.after: The client keeps bounded transient answers and replaces an existing answer of the same identity rather than accumulating duplicates.
limits: The recorded frame/control result is one fixture, not the configured limit or a whole-process memory guarantee.
Screen-reader/physical scrolling acceptance remains separate.

items.title: Deleting messages in private channels is faster
items.summary: When the server sends live updates to connected people, it now shares the checks on who may see them across one batch of updates. The shared checks last only for that batch.
items.before: Deleting messages in a private channel rebuilt the list of who could see it for every message, even when no one was online. Several devices signed in to the same session repeated the same session check.
items.after: If no one is online, deleting a batch of private messages reads no list of readers. If people are online, the batch reads the channel's members once and still tells every device about each deleted message.
items.mechanism: Gateway visits connected byUser recipients, memoizes session checks only within the publication and server batches replaceable recounts; it does not introduce long-lived authorization cache.

limits: Measured on one Linux computer. Real times depend on how many members and readers a channel has, and on the disk.
The server still checks membership and removed access every time. If a check fails, it disconnects that session and sends it nothing that relied on the check.

technical.title: Avoid offline/repeated publication authorization and recount work
technical.summary: Fan-out shares short-lived authorization/audience work inside a committed synchronous publication batch.
technical.before: Private deletion rebuilt a channel's audience per event even with no readers; multiple devices of the same session repeated the same session lookup.
technical.after: Offline private batches read no audience, and online batches share one channel read while still sending every durable deletion frame.
limits: Single Linux host; actual timing depends on membership, readers and storage.
Membership/revocation checks remain authoritative; failed authorization closes the affected session and sends no dependent frame.

items.title: Telling outside apps about events repeats less work
items.summary: When one app has many event subscriptions, the server now checks that app and the channel once per event and builds the shared part of the notice once.
items.before: One event with 100 subscriptions repeated the same membership check, workspace lookup and notice building 100 times.
items.after: Each subscription still gets its own delivery, saved on the server. The shared checks, lookup and notice building run once.
items.mechanism: Group event preparation by bot/channel within the event, retain per-subscription filtering/admission/redaction, then insert the distinct delivery jobs.

metrics.label: Posting a message with 100 subscriptions, typical time, repeated runs
Times the shared checks, lookup and notice building run

limits: With one or ten subscriptions there was no clear change in time. Saving each delivery is still needed.
Measured on one computer. It does not claim how many apps a server can handle.

technical.title: Share integration eligibility and payload construction per event
technical.summary: One bot with many subscriptions reuses the same bot/channel eligibility and common event envelope.
technical.before: One event with 100 subscriptions repeated identical membership, workspace metadata and JSON serialization work 100 times.
technical.after: Distinct subscriptions still get their own durable delivery rows, but shared checks/read/body construction run once.
limits: No clear timing change at one or ten subscriptions; row writes remain necessary.
Single-host measured result is not a general integration capacity claim.

items.title: Desktop backups load only the backup code they need
items.summary: The desktop app's background jobs that back up, check, list and restore the workspace now load only the backup code.
items.before: These jobs loaded the whole server, including its networking parts, even though they only needed to work with the database and files.
items.after: The background job's code was measured at 44,577 bytes. Backup and restore passed their checks in the packaged desktop app.
items.mechanism: Move version/build constants to a light server module and export a dedicated backup entry; worker imports it directly and returns only result/error metadata.
limits: An early trial measured 684,998 bytes down to 38,858, and 180.66 milliseconds down to 74.46. That was not the final build, so no overall speedup of the jobs is claimed.
When the desktop app runs the server, ordinary database work still happens in the part of the app that manages its windows. Whether to move it elsewhere will be decided later, based on measurements.

technical.title: Keep heavy backup SQL off main and keep workers dependency-light
technical.summary: Desktop backup/verify/inventory/restore workers import only the focused backup module.
technical.before: Full server-barrel imports pulled networking dependencies into jobs that only needed database/filesystem backup work.
technical.after: The emitted focused worker was verified at 44,577 bytes and packaged backup/restore paths passed their controls.
limits: The earlier 684,998→38,858-byte and 180.66→74.46-ms candidate probe is not the final emitted-build measurement; no final total-job speedup is claimed here.
Ordinary embedded-server queries still run synchronously in Electron main; backend isolation remains an evidence-led future decision.

items.title: Deleted files get cleaned up even when some removals fail
items.summary: When removing a deleted file from disk fails, the server now remembers it, even across restarts, and waits longer before trying again. Failures can no longer block the files behind them.
items.before: A hundred files that could never be removed could keep a 101st, removable file waiting, even after a restart. Each batch of removable files also waited for a 15 second timer.
items.after: Removable files keep being cleaned up in later rounds. Failed ones wait longer between tries, up to two hours. Files with broken names that can never be removed are set aside where people can see them.
items.mechanism: Stable due ordering uses queue time, attempts and next-attempt time; backoff grows through one minute, five, thirty and two hours. File bytes remain accounted until physical deletion succeeds.
limits: This keeps cleanup moving and makes it correct. It does not claim that working with files got faster.
Files that can never be removed stay visible, and the space they use is not counted as freed.

technical.title: Make attachment removal fair and promptly drain healthy backlog
technical.summary: Schema v35 gives failed blob removals persistent eligibility/backoff so they cannot monopolize the first page.
technical.before: One hundred permanently failing paths could keep a healthy 101st blob queued across restart; healthy pages waited for each 15-second timer.
technical.after: Healthy removals continue on bounded later turns while individual failures back off, and permanent malformed names are visibly set aside.
limits: This improves cleanup progress and correctness; no generic filesystem speedup is asserted.
Permanent failures remain visible and reserved storage is not falsely reclaimed.

items.title: The web version loads faster on a slow connection
items.summary: The server sends compressed copies of the web version's files, made once ahead of time. Browsers keep files that never change for a year instead of checking them on every visit.
items.before: The server sent the web version's files uncompressed, and browsers checked unchanged files again on every visit. Compressing each file on request would have cost the server work every time.
items.after: Browsers get a compressed copy made ahead of time. Files named after their contents are kept in the browser for a year. The main page is still checked each visit, and a request for a file from an old version gets a clear 'not found' that browsers do not keep.
items.mechanism: Vite writes quality-11 Brotli/level-9 gzip sidecars once; @fastify/static serves variants with Vary. Integrity guards decode every copy and compare it to source.

technical.title: Serve precompressed assets and reuse hashed browser files
technical.summary: Build-time Brotli/gzip and immutable hashed-asset caching reduce repeated-host delivery work and cold bytes.
technical.before: Hosts sent uncompressed client text and revalidated unchanged scripts with every visit; compressing at request time would add recurring CPU work.
technical.after: Browsers negotiate prebuilt variants, hashed assets cache for a year, the page revalidates, and missing old chunks return explicit 404/no-store.

Warm visible-control timing was effectively unchanged around 985 ms; API/attachment compression was not changed.

items.title: The desktop app leaves out files it never reads
items.summary: The desktop app no longer packs the source files meant for developers that come with the libraries it uses. The code that runs, the details it needs and the licenses stay.
items.before: The desktop app's packed files still included developer source files inside its libraries, which the app never loads.
items.after: The packed files on Linux are smaller. Builds with and without the change both still run the libraries, the server and backups correctly.
items.mechanism: Electron Builder excludes those extensions under node_modules; the archive guard rejects their accidental reintroduction.

The app never read the removed files, so no faster start or lower memory use is claimed.

technical.title: Prune dependency TypeScript from the desktop package
technical.summary: Remove unused .ts/.cts/.mts files from packaged dependencies while preserving runtime JS, required metadata and licenses.
technical.before: The clean desktop ASAR still carried TypeScript sources/declarations inside node_modules that Node never loads there.
technical.after: Linux archive payload is smaller; both filtered and unfiltered packages retain working dependency/server/backup paths.
limits: Package-size gain only. Launch 1.42–1.46 s, hosting 1.48–1.53 s and memory ranges were indistinguishable between packages.
The excluded files were never read, so no startup or memory benefit is claimed.

items.title: Checks on each change skip work they already did
items.summary: The checks that run on every change now reuse earlier results when nothing they depend on changed. They also run fewer jobs at once and build the Windows installer only when it matters.
items.before: Separate steps each rebuilt the web version, test runs crowded each other, and every change to the app's code built a Windows installer that the desktop tests never used.
items.after: Saved results are tied to every source, settings and test file they depend on. Ordinary changes build the Windows app without its installer, and changes that could affect the installer still build it.
items.mechanism: Cache task outputs separately from dependency/browser downloads; run cache/format/bundle/browser guards independently, limit task/Vitest concurrency and fail safe to full packaging when the base diff is unavailable.

15 mutation / 101 hash assertion guard
