metrics.label: Checks that saved results are thrown away when they should be

limits: The 1.09 seconds leaves out installing, downloading saved results, formatting checks, browser setup and full app tests. It is not the total time of a check run on GitHub.
Building the installer used to take 73 to 89 seconds. That is the work expected to be skipped, not a measured saving.
Who can use saved results, and throwing them away at the right time, still matter. Saved results are not a security safeguard.

technical.title: Reuse verified task outputs and avoid unused installer stages
technical.summary: Content-addressed Turbo reuse, bounded concurrency and installer-aware selection reduce redundant validation work.
technical.before: Independent commands rebuilt web output, package worker pools overlapped, and every Windows runtime PR generated an installer that native tests did not use.
technical.after: Task hashes cover complete source/config/test inputs; ordinary runtime PRs build unpacked Windows output while installer-sensitive changes retain NSIS.
limits: 1.09 s excludes install/cache transfer, formatting, browser setup and E2E; it is not total Actions duration.
Recorded 73–89 s prior installer stages describe expected avoided work, not a measured new remote saving.
Cache scope/permissions and correct invalidation remain essential; task caches are not a security boundary.

items.title: Server package rebuilds reuse unchanged libraries
items.summary: When building the ready-to-run Docker package of the server, the build downloads the exact library versions before copying in Tandem's own code. It installs only the libraries the server ships with.
items.before: Any change to Tandem's code made the build copy the whole project and reinstall every library.
items.after: Edits to Tandem's own code can reuse the downloaded and installed libraries. Changes to the list of library versions, the build tools or the install rules start fresh on purpose.
items.mechanism: Multi-stage Node 24 image uses pnpm fetch, offline frozen filtered installation, stamped server/web builds and BuildKit Actions layer reuse. Final image copies only dist and runs as a non-root user.

evidence.label: Actual separated layers
Layer cache and smoke/reuse checks

limits: No before and after build time is claimed. The Windows computer used for the research could not run Linux Docker builds.
The checks on every change still restart the server with its saved data, test its live connection and test that build steps are reused.

technical.title: Separate lockfile dependency work from source-layer builds
technical.summary: Container builds fetch pinned packages before copying source and install only the shipped dependency closure.
technical.before: Any source change invalidated a stage that copied the whole repository before installation.
technical.after: Source-only edits can reuse dependency fetch/install inputs; lock/toolchain/install-policy changes intentionally invalidate them.
limits: No local before/after image timing is asserted; the documented Windows research environment lacked a usable Linux Docker engine.
Persistent-volume restart/socket and reuse smoke controls remain part of CI.

items.title: Tests and releases always match the current code
items.summary: Each build is stamped with what it was built from. Tests refuse old or broken builds, and release files come as a fixed set, each with a fingerprint that can be checked.
items.before: Browser and desktop tests could start an old leftover build. A badly formed build stamp could cause a confusing failure. Preparing a release twice could record the fingerprint of old release notes before rewriting them.
items.after: Tests refuse builds that are missing, out of date or badly stamped, and say how to rebuild. Images and other non-text files are fingerprinted byte for byte, and release files are a chosen set, each tied to its fingerprint.
items.mechanism: One identity module supplies version/revision/dirty/input hashes to web/server/desktop, manifests and diagnostics; install gates inspect the actual app's profile report.

evidence.label: Identity mutation and malformed-manifest controls

limits: This makes test results more trustworthy. It does not make the app faster.
Upgrading from a real published version, and publishing a real release, still need their own checks. A test package without a signature does not prove that a signed release works.

technical.title: Bind tests and releases to matching source artifacts
technical.summary: Stamped source-input identities, archive checks and repeatable release manifests prevent stale/unclean output from giving false test confidence.
technical.before: Browser/native tests could launch leftover bundles, malformed identities could fail badly, and repeated release preparation could checksum old notes before rewriting them.
technical.after: Tests reject missing/stale/malformed output with rebuild guidance; binary inputs are hashed exactly and release assets are a deliberate hash-bound set.
limits: Assurance improvement, not a runtime speed claim.
A genuine upgrade from a published release and a real publication remain explicit acceptance work; unsigned packaging is not signed release proof.

items.title: Speed tests only count work that actually succeeded
items.summary: The scripts that time the server under mixed use, and the browser at startup and while scrolling images, now record the code version, test data, computer, samples and errors.
items.before: Earlier mixed-use tests could skip actually deleting old messages, accept an incomplete catch-up, and keep test leftovers that muddied the memory and freeze readings.
items.after: The mixed-use test now creates messages that are exactly due for deletion, checks that they are deleted, and checks that catch-up arrives complete and in order. It limits what the test itself holds on to, and records how much work it asked for and how much finished.
items.mechanism: Workload scripts check correctness before/while timing; artifacts report latency distributions and scope rather than timing an error as successful work.
limits: These are tools and starting measurements. They do not make anything faster or claim how much a server can handle.
Past results from cloud computers and from browsers with no window do not show how the desktop app runs on a slow computer. Measuring on a chosen reference computer is still to do.

technical.title: Make performance decisions from successful reproducible work
technical.summary: Server mixed-load and browser startup/image-scroll scripts record revision, fixture, host/runtime, samples and errors.
technical.before: Earlier mixed probes could skip actual retention, accept incomplete replay and retain harness state that confounded memory/stalls.
technical.after: F12 seeds exact expired data, verifies deletion and ordered replay/snapshot, bounds receipts/sockets and records offered/completed load.
limits: These are measurement tools and baselines, not optimization speedups or declared capacity.
Historical mixed/cloud/headless results must not be treated as low-spec desktop-main/GPU acceptance; reference-hardware profiling remains open.

items.title: A garbled web address can no longer break server logging
items.summary: When a request's web address has a garbled setting name, the server can still write the request to its log.
items.before: If a web address had a garbled name in its settings part, the step that hides secrets before logging could fail and break logging for that request.
items.after: The server hides the garbled name and its value in the log, and keeps answering later requests.
items.mechanism: Catch query-name decoding failure before classifying sensitive parameters, mask both sides, and retain ordinary secret redaction.

evidence.label: Actual child-process survival regression

limits: The test proves the server survives this kind of garbled address. It claims no speed gain and does not say how often this happened in real use.

technical.title: Make malformed query logging safe
technical.summary: Invalid percent-encoded query names cannot terminate request logging.
technical.before: A malformed query name could throw while being decoded by the redactor and escape the logging path.
technical.after: Malformed names and their values are masked; the real child server keeps answering later requests.
limits: The regression proves the tested malformed-input boundary; no timing gain or natural crash frequency is claimed.

items.title: Web drafts survive storage errors and several open tabs
items.summary: If the browser's storage fails, the web version says so and can try again. Changes cut off midway are finished on the next start, finished ones are never applied twice, and several open tabs keep each other's work.
items.before: If the browser's main storage failed to open, the web version could quietly switch to a simpler storage area that was empty. Whether the browser let tabs signal each other could change which storage was used. Older copies of drafts could overwrite private choices or newer work.
items.after: The app records that it uses the main storage before it starts using it. If the main storage will not open, the app refuses to write anywhere else and can try again later. Old drafts, messages waiting to send and privacy choices that disagree are merged with care.
items.mechanism: Transactions serialize updates across independent contexts. Persistent operation IDs/tombstones prevent stale replay; legacy draft conflicts retain both texts, outbox removals remain removed and privacy reconciliation chooses the more private value. Storage-event/focus invalidation works without BroadcastChannel and carries no private payload.

evidence.label: Recovery, denied ownership and local-only watcher controls

limits: Saving in the browser does not protect against the computer losing power.
A new browser profile with no main storage can use the simpler storage area. Once the main storage has been used, the app never falls back to the simpler one.
Four related findings, about the order in which accounts, preferences and sign-in are handled, are separate. This change does not fix them. All four were repaired later.

technical.title: Keep one durable browser storage owner and recover conflicts
technical.summary: IndexedDB failures remain visible/retryable, unfinished operations stay journaled and acknowledged operations are not reapplied, and multi-window recovery preserves local work.
technical.before: Failed IndexedDB opening could silently switch to empty localStorage; optional BroadcastChannel absence could alter backend choice; older migration copies could overwrite private/local work.
technical.after: Ownership is persisted before adoption, opening failure refuses alternate-backend writes, later calls can retry, and old conflicting drafts/outbox/privacy choices reconcile safely.
limits: Browser storage is not an OS power-loss guarantee.
Fresh profiles without IndexedDB can use localStorage until adoption; acknowledged IndexedDB ownership prevents later alternate fallback.
Q02/Q03/Q04/Q05 are caller-level identity/preference/sign-in ordering findings this backend fix does not close; all four were closed separately.

items.title: Your last words typed are saved when the desktop app closes
items.summary: Closing a desktop window or quitting the app now waits until the text on screen, other unsaved work and the app's settings are saved.
items.before: The last few keystrokes you could see might exist only on the screen. When closing the window threw the page away, they were lost.
items.after: A normal close saves the current text and waits until it is confirmed as saved. If saving fails, you can still copy the text, try again or choose to quit without saving.
items.mechanism: Composer captures through layout cleanup, DraftPersistence drains restore/pending/failed/recovery work, preload sends a matching preparation reply, and main drains settings behind a window/request-bound handshake.

evidence.label: Foreign/stale reply, failure and timeout controls

limits: Tested with a normal close and quit on a Windows build of the app. A force-quit, signing out of the computer and power loss are separate cases.

technical.title: Save the visible final composer text before native exit
technical.summary: Desktop window close/quit waits for current UI text, pending local work and the native settings queue.
technical.before: The last visible keystrokes could exist only in the renderer when native close destroyed the page.
technical.after: Normal close captures current text and acknowledges persistence before destruction; failure keeps copying/retry/explicit unsaved exit available.
limits: Normal app close/quit verified on unpacked Windows output; forced process death, OS logoff and physical power loss are separate conditions.

items.title: Calls keep your latest mute choice
items.summary: Swapping in a microphone, and both ways of joining a call, now follow your latest saved mute choice.
items.before: A microphone the app had kept or recovered could pick up an older, unmuted setting. One way of joining could start before your saved setting had loaded.
items.after: A new microphone takes your current mute choice. Joining waits for your setting to load or finish saving. If the setting cannot be read, you join muted and the app tries again.
items.mechanism: Separate intent from the physical track. Preference generations fence late older reads against newer retries/saves and lifetime checks prevent canceled/unmounted join completion.

evidence.label: Held preference, muted join and entry-point regressions

limits: Tests used fake microphones. Unplugging a real one, choosing a real device and calling someone on another network still need their own checks.

technical.title: Apply the latest mute intent when adopting a microphone
technical.summary: Track replacement and both join entry points honor current acknowledged microphone preferences.
technical.before: Held/recovered capture could adopt an older unmuted value; a join route could run before preference initialization settled.
technical.after: Replacement tracks use the current desired-mute state; joins await the current initialization/save and unreadable preference state keeps capture muted with retry.
limits: Synthetic media/held-capture controls do not establish physical unplug, real device selection or second-network calling acceptance.

items.title: An old app form can no longer change a new one
items.summary: When an app's form is closed or replaced, the result of an earlier submission can no longer reach the new form.
items.before: An old form's success, a refusal of what you typed or a network failure could close the new form that replaced it, or mix wrong details into it.
items.after: What you type, field errors and the busy sign belong to the form on screen. Only that form's own submission can update or close it.
items.mechanism: Key AppForm by view ID, guard component/submission lifetime, and fence WorkspaceClient submit/dismiss actions by the modal identity.

evidence.label: Real app callback/socket lifetime regression

limits: This covers what the form on screen does. Two submissions reaching the server at almost the same moment, and an app acting twice on one submission, are handled separately by repair N08.

technical.title: Give each app form its own asynchronous lifetime
technical.summary: A dismissed or replaced app form cannot receive an older submission's state or completion effects.
technical.before: An old form's success, validation refusal or network failure could close or contaminate a replacement form.
technical.after: Input, field errors and busy state belong to the active view; only that view's live request can update or close it.
limits: This owns UI/modal completion; server concurrent submission and external-effect deduplication are separate N08 limits.

items.title: Deleted messages no longer keep their button contents
items.summary: When a message is deleted, the server now also removes its buttons' labels, values and links. This applies to the marker left in its place and to older copies kept for catching up.
items.before: Deleting or replacing a message cleared its text, but its buttons could still hold content from the person or app.
items.after: Deleted messages and old copies kept for catching up carry no button content. Buttons on current messages stay as they are.
items.mechanism: Set actions to an empty array during soft deletion and replay redaction, then schema v37 cleans existing deleted/purged/superseded active database records.

evidence.label: Current-action preservation and historical-copy cleanup

limits: The cleanup does not erase old backups, or leftover data in disk space the database has freed but not yet overwritten.

technical.title: Strip action content from deleted and superseded message copies
technical.summary: Deletion cleanup now removes interactive button labels, values and URLs from active tombstones and superseded replay events.
technical.before: Text was cleaned while action payloads could retain user/app content after deletion or replacement.
technical.after: Deleted rows and old replay copies carry no action payload; current live message buttons remain intact.
limits: Active-record cleanup does not erase historical backups or freed SQLite disk pages.

items.title: Sent scheduled messages no longer keep a copy of their text
items.summary: Once a scheduled message has been sent, the server no longer keeps a second copy of its text and its list of files in the record of scheduled messages.
items.before: After a scheduled message went out, the server still kept its text and its links to attached files in the scheduled list, even though nothing needed them anymore.
items.after: A sent scheduled message keeps only its status, its times and which message it became. Older sent records are cleared the same way when the server updates. Scheduled messages that have not gone out yet keep everything they need to send.
items.mechanism: On completion write empty text and file_ids, and schema v37 migrates old sent rows under the same content-minimization policy.

evidence.label: Sent cleanup and queued preservation controls

limits: This is about privacy and not keeping text longer than needed. It does not claim a smaller database or a faster server.
Older backups still contain the removed text, and freeing the disk space it used is not part of this change.

technical.title: Remove completed schedule content while retaining completion metadata
technical.summary: Completed scheduled messages no longer keep a redundant text/file-ID copy in the schedule table.
technical.before: An already-sent schedule still retained message text and attachment references after its delivery purpose ended.
technical.after: Sent rows keep state/timing/completion identity without text or attachment IDs; queued unsent schedules retain what delivery requires.
limits: Removing duplicate schedule content is a privacy/storage-lifecycle fix; no measured database-size or throughput saving is claimed.
Historical backups and freed bytes remain outside this cleanup.

items.title: An app form cannot be sent twice at the same moment
items.summary: When an app opens a form in Tandem, only one submission of that form can be on its way to the app at a time. Once the app answers, the person can fix mistakes or send it again.
items.before: Two submissions of the same form at almost the same moment could both reach the outside app.
items.after: A second submission while the first is still on its way is refused with a note to wait for the app's answer. Fixing a field the app flagged, or deliberately trying again after a failed connection, still works.
items.mechanism: A per-view submitting Set is acquired before callback dispatch and released in finally; view/account ownership is validated independently.

evidence.label: Concurrent, correction, independent-view and owner controls

limits: This stops two submissions at the same moment. If the network fails and nobody knows whether the app got the form, sending it again can still make the app act twice. Apps should use the form's ID to skip a repeat.

technical.title: Exclude simultaneous duplicate app view submissions
technical.summary: One app view can have only one callback in flight, with correction/retry available after it settles.
technical.before: Concurrent requests for the same view could both reach the external application.
technical.after: A second active submission gets 409 view_submitting, while later validation correction and deliberate transport retry still work.
limits: The Set prevents simultaneous dispatch, not exactly-once external business effects after an uncertain network reply. Apps should deduplicate by view ID.

items.title: A late app reply cannot change an edited or deleted message
items.summary: When an app answers a button press late, it can no longer replace or delete a message that was removed or changed after the press.
items.before: If the message was edited or deleted at almost the same moment, a late instruction from the app could still replace or delete the newer version.
items.after: If the message is gone or has changed since the button was pressed, a late replace or delete does nothing. An app can still update its own message several times in a row through the same reply link.
items.mechanism: Hash origin text/editedAt/actions, compare before mutation and advance the shared origin revision after a valid self-update.

evidence.label: Delayed edit/delete and same-response chain controls

limits: The check covers the message's text, when it was last edited and its buttons. It is not a general way to keep every change in order across devices.

technical.title: Fence delayed app replace/delete directives to their origin revision
technical.summary: An old response URL cannot replace/delete a message that disappeared or was changed since its callback origin.
technical.before: Late directives could act on the message's newer state after an edit/deletion race.
technical.after: Missing or changed origins make delayed replace/delete a no-op; an app can continue its own update chain through the same response URL.
limits: The fingerprint covers the declared message fields; it is not a general cross-device revision protocol for all state.

items.title: Removing an old thread also clears its files from the app
items.summary: When the server's automatic history removal deletes a whole thread, the app now clears its copies of files from the first message and every reply, even if those replies were never loaded.
items.before: Saved copies of a removed thread's files, or downloads of them still in progress, could outlive the thread. The app did not know which files belonged to the replies because it had not loaded them.
items.after: The app drops its copies of the thread's files and stops their downloads. A download that finishes late cannot put them back. A file preview that is open says the file is no longer available.
items.mechanism: File ownership includes threadRootId independent of loaded history. history.removed invalidates those owners; unknown-owner entries are conservatively revalidated on removal.

evidence.label: Held-transfer and evicted-owner regressions

limits: The server already refused to send these files again. This fix clears copies the app had already fetched.
Files someone already downloaded or copied elsewhere cannot be taken back.

technical.title: Invalidate cached attachment bytes when a whole thread is retained away
technical.summary: Retention removal reaches root and reply attachment ownership even after history eviction.
technical.before: Cached blob URLs or held transfers could outlive a thread removed by retention because reply ownership was absent from the loaded history.
technical.after: Root/reply bytes are canceled/released, a late transfer cannot reinstall them, and an active preview explains unavailability.
limits: Fresh server authorization already denied unavailable files; this fixes previously fetched local resources.
Previously downloaded/copied content cannot be retroactively unrevealed.

items.title: A restored backup stays on hold even with damaged settings
items.summary: After a restore, the desktop app keeps the restored copy on hold, open only for looking inside from this computer. Damaged details in the app's settings can no longer lift that hold.
items.before: If the app's saved name, port or date for a restored copy was damaged, the app dropped that entry. It could then pick up the folder again as an ordinary workspace, losing the hold that kept it apart.
items.after: The hold survives damage to the name, port or date, which can be repaired. If the app cannot tell which workspace is on hold, it refuses to host it. The app still adds new workspace folders it finds, as before.
items.mechanism: Parse safety-critical identity/hold metadata independently of optional presentation fields and fail closed when a held folder/identity cannot be established.

evidence.label: Damaged metadata and adoption regressions

limits: This fixes how the app picks up folders. Keeping other servers out while a restore swaps folders was a separate repair.

technical.title: Preserve restored-copy holds despite damaged registry metadata
technical.summary: Malformed display fields cannot cause a held restored workspace to be adopted into ordinary hosting.
technical.before: A damaged name, port or timestamp could discard a registry row and lose the protection that kept a restored copy isolated.
technical.after: Hold state survives recoverable display damage; uncertain held identities remain blocked while ordinary new-folder adoption stays supported.
limits: This closes registry-adoption behavior; Q01 separately closed the restore publication lock gap.

items.title: A public link that fails to close is not forgotten
items.summary: When opening a workspace to the internet is canceled or fails, the desktop app keeps track of the public link until it has really closed.
items.before: If closing the public link failed, the app could treat it as closed. You could then open another link or change who can join while the old link was still running.
items.after: A link that did not close stays marked as needing cleanup, and the app keeps hold of it. The app will not open another link until stopping hosting finishes the cleanup. Waiting for a link to close has a time limit and can be tried again.
items.mechanism: TunnelCleanupError carries the connector to the controller, including canceled/setup-failed handles and accidental-port isolated listeners. Cleanup waits are bounded and retryable; established close failures also mark pending cleanup.

evidence.label: Connector teardown controls

limits: The tests faked these failures on this computer. They do not show how often a real public link is left running.
Two related problems were repaired separately. A server could keep running unseen after its invite setting failed, and stopping could wait behind a backup before cleanup began.

technical.title: Retain connector/server ownership until cleanup actually succeeds
technical.summary: Canceled/failed public setup cannot abandon handles that still need teardown.
technical.before: An unsuccessful connector close could be treated as finished, allowing another route/access change while the old resource remained alive.
technical.after: Failed cleanup stays pending, resource handles remain owned and reopening is gated until retry establishes cleanup.
limits: Loopback/injected connector failures do not establish a real Cloudflare orphan frequency.
Q12 and Q13 separately closed the main-adapter handle gap after listening and the pre-cleanup queue wait.

items.title: Fixed limits on loaded messages, files and slow connections
items.summary: Tandem already limits how much history and how many file copies the app holds, and the server sends files without loading each one whole into memory.
items.before: Without limits, long histories, the same file fetched twice at once, or data piling up for a slow connection would make memory use grow the longer someone stays and the busier the server gets.
items.after: A channel or thread keeps at most 300 messages loaded. The app keeps at most 20 of each kind of conversation you are not viewing. Files not on screen share 32 megabytes. At most four files download at once. The server cuts off a connection that falls 2 megabytes behind, and that device reconnects and catches up.
items.mechanism: LRU eviction protects active histories, file fetches deduplicate/cancel, image bodies load near the viewport, streaming server transfers preserve bounded body work, and reconnect uses durable replay/snapshot fallback.
limits: These are set limits, not measurements of speed or memory.

Files on screen, images once unpacked for display, the full copy of a workspace sent when a device connects, the total number of connections, and the disk space the server uses for its database and temporary files each need their own limits and testing.

technical.title: Keep history, attachment transfer and socket work bounded
technical.summary: The architecture already caps retained page/cache work and avoids materializing whole file bodies during transfer.
technical.before: Unbounded histories, independent duplicate file fetches or unchecked socket buffering would scale memory with session duration/load.
technical.after: Timeline/thread windows hold 300 messages, inactive caches have 20 entries per category, idle blobs have a 32 MiB budget, body fetches have four slots and slow sockets use a 2 MiB queued-byte cutoff.
limits: These are configured bounds, not comparative speed/memory measurements.
Active blobs, decoded pixels, complete account snapshots, aggregate connections and database/WAL/staging storage need separate budgets and profiling.

items.title: A failed background job no longer crashes the server
items.summary: Errors in the server's background work, such as sending scheduled messages, delivering events to apps and timers, or in its live connections, no longer stop the whole server.
items.before: A failed disk read or other error inside background work, or while keeping a live connection open and handling its messages, could stop the server for everyone.
items.after: Background work that fails stays saved and is tried again on a later round. If the server cannot check that a connection is still signed in, it sends nothing that depends on that check and closes the connection so the device can reconnect.
items.mechanism: Contain synchronous/asynchronous whole entry boundaries, report bounded queue failure metadata, deduplicate session checks within a batch and let explicit operational flush callers still learn that work failed.
limits: The tests caused these failures on purpose. They show the server survives and recovers, not how often real disks fail.
The saved list of jobs still decides what remains to be done, and a change that failed to save is never announced as done.

technical.title: Contain background jobs and socket callback failures
technical.summary: Actual scheduled/delivery/timer and Gateway callback faults no longer escape as unhandled process-ending work.
technical.before: Read/rejection faults through native interval/immediate callbacks or socket heartbeat/message/close could terminate the host.
technical.after: Queue failures retain durable rows and retry on later turns; unreadable session authorization sends no dependent frame and closes for recovery.
limits: Fault injection establishes survival/correct recovery at these boundaries, not the frequency of real disk failures.
Durable jobs remain authoritative and no transaction failure is treated as accepted publication.

items.title: Retries to apps are kept, and a slow app delays no others
items.summary: When an administrator asks to retry events an app missed, Tandem keeps that request within the limit on waiting events. Apps that answer normally keep receiving events while another app is slow.
items.before: A retry could put 1,500 events into a line that holds 500. The cleanup that drops given-up events after seven days could erase a retry someone had asked for. One slow app held back deliveries to unrelated apps.
items.after: Retried events join the line as space frees up. The request to retry survives a restart and the seven-day cleanup. Healthy apps keep receiving events while another one is held back.
items.mechanism: Schema v36 records retry_requested; terminal-history pruning excludes accepted requested retry intent. The pump has at most ten concurrent operations and one per subscription, preserving per-subscription order.
limits: Retried events go out oldest first among themselves, after events that were already waiting. They are not put back in their original place in history.

If an app's answer was unclear, the app may act on the same event twice. Overall limits on how many events, or how much data, may wait for all apps together are not set yet and depend on how the server is run.

technical.title: Keep accepted integration retry intent and healthy endpoint progress
technical.summary: Durable repair intent respects admission limits/expiry, and independent endpoints refill freed delivery slots without a slow-peer barrier.
technical.before: Retry could restore 1,500 rows into a 500-row ready queue; seven-day pruning could erase accepted waiting intent; one slow endpoint held back unrelated work.
technical.after: A bounded ready queue promotes requested retries as space frees, retains requested intent through restart/expiry, and healthy endpoints advance while another remains held.
limits: Retry replay is ordered within its subset after already queued events, not globally inserted back into historical sequence order.
Uncertain external responses can repeat consumer effects; global integration count/byte budgets are still an operating-envelope decision.

items.title: Losing access clears a channel even when a notice fails
items.summary: When someone is removed from a channel, their open app no longer keeps showing it just because the server's notice to their device failed.
items.before: The server already refused new requests from the removed person. But if the notice to their open app failed, it kept showing the channel and its history until they reconnected by hand.
items.after: If that notice fails, the server makes the affected devices reconnect. When they do, the app drops the channel and its history. The removal still counts, and the person who made it still sees it succeed.
items.mechanism: Target affected sessions for reconnect after access-state fan-out failure instead of rolling back a durable mutation or suppressing later events.
limits: This clears what the device had already loaded once it reconnects. It cannot undo anything already downloaded, and it gives no new access.

technical.title: Reconnect affected clients after failed access publication
technical.summary: Committed revocation cannot leave the affected device indefinitely relying on stale cached access solely because its refresh notice failed.
technical.before: Fresh HTTP correctly refused the removed user, but failed post-commit publication left its existing client showing old channel/history until manual reconnect.
technical.after: Failure triggers resynchronization of the affected devices; handshake clears the revoked channel/history and preserves committed HTTP success.
limits: This removes previously fetched state after resynchronization; it does not undo data already downloaded or grant fresh unauthorized access.

items.title: Quick pin, save and snooze changes end on your last choice
items.summary: Pins, saved messages, Do Not Disturb snoozes and channel notification choices now go to the server one at a time and end on your latest choice. A workspace the app has closed sends nothing more.
items.before: Two quick changes could reach the server in the wrong order, so the older one won. Leftover work from a workspace the app had just closed could also overwrite the choice made after reopening it.
items.after: The app sends one change at a time for each item. Your latest choice waits for the one already on its way, then goes out. When the app closes a workspace, it drops changes still waiting and refuses new ones.
items.mechanism: Per-item queues keep one request active, send the latest queued choice after it settles and guard corrections/echo reconciliation by client lifetime.
limits: A change already on its way to the server cannot be called back. Keeping changes from two devices in order still needs help from the server.
Following a thread had its own problem, where Follow then Unfollow could end followed. This fix does not cover it, and it was repaired separately.

technical.title: Serialize local choice writes and stop queued work after destruction
technical.summary: Pins, saved items, snooze and preference choices have one active local write, a coalesced latest choice and explicit client lifetime.
technical.before: Reordered parallel writes or an old destroyed client's repair could overwrite its replacement client's newer choice.
technical.after: Latest intent waits behind the in-flight request; destroy drops queued/repair work and refuses new writes.
limits: An already-delivered request cannot be recalled; cross-device ordering still needs a server revision contract.
Follow has a different ordering boundary, not covered by this pin/save/snooze implementation; Q09 closed it separately.

items.title: The desktop app reloads a crashed window and keeps hosting
items.summary: If the desktop app's window crashes or fails to load, the app reloads it on its own a few times and puts you back where you were.
items.before: A crashed window could stay blank. Early recovery brought back the channel but lost whether you were in Saved, a thread, a side panel or a search.
items.after: Up to three failures in a minute reload the window on its own. After that, the app shows a Try again button. A workspace this computer hosts keeps running throughout, and the place you were is checked and handed back once.
items.mechanism: Separate renderer lifetime from native service ownership and retain a bounded trusted URL/history checkpoint outside renderer memory.

evidence.label: Actual retry and checkpoint policy

limits: The place you return to is checked against your account and workspace. It does not bring back local work you are no longer allowed to see.
Whether recent changes survive a crash or a power cut still depends on separate limits on what is saved to disk.

technical.title: Recover a failed renderer without stopping its host
technical.summary: Electron retries a crashed/failed page within a bounded budget and restores its validated route/history context.
technical.before: Renderer failures could leave a blank page; early retry restoration kept channel but lost Saved/thread/panel/query context.
technical.after: Up to three failures in a minute reload automatically, followed by Try again/explicit action; main-side hosting remains alive and valid place state is handed back once.
limits: Recovered route state is validated against the account/workspace; it does not revive unauthorised local work.
Crash/power-loss durability remains subject to the separate acknowledged storage boundaries.

items.title: A server starting mid-restore can no longer take the workspace folder
items.summary: Restoring a backup has to let go of the workspace folder for a moment to swap in the restored copy. It now keeps a second claim, held beside the folder, until the swap is done, so nothing else can start there meanwhile.
items.before: Restore let go of the folder just before the swap. A server that started at that moment made a new, empty workspace in its place. The restore then failed, and the original workspace was left in a set-aside folder.
items.after: A server or a second restore that asks for the folder during a restore is refused, also when the folder is not there yet. If the swap fails, the original goes back where it was. The extra claim leaves nothing beside the folder once it is let go.
items.mechanism: Hold a path lock beside the target through staging, both renames and rollback; every folder hold asks for it before making or locking the folder; its file is removed on release by a holder certain of the file's identity.

evidence.label: A server start and a second restore at each point of the swap, and a failed swap
The path held with no folder, by another process, and cleaned up after

limits: A server from a version before this one does not ask for the new claim, so it can still slip in during a swap.
Where the server may not write beside its folder, as in the container image, the extra claim is skipped. A restore cannot swap folders there either.
The claim goes by the folder's address, so the same folder reached through a link has a separate one.
A power cut between the two moves of the swap still leaves no folder at the address, with the original set aside.

technical.title: Keep exclusive restore admission through folder publication
technical.summary: Restore holds a sibling path lock across staging, both renames and rollback, and holdWorkspace takes the same lock before it makes or locks the folder.
technical.before: Restore released the in-folder lock before renaming. A concurrent createWorkspaceServer could mkdir the absent target; publication then failed and rollback could not overwrite the new target.
technical.after: holdWorkspacePath locks <dataDir>.lock with SQLite BEGIN IMMEDIATE and an in-memory journal. Concurrent starts and restores get WorkspaceInUseError without creating the folder, including for a target that does not exist yet; a failed install renames the superseded folder back while the path is still held. The lock file is removed on release: after close on Windows, where an open file cannot be removed, and under the lock elsewhere, with a dev/inode/birthtime comparison on acquisition that rejects a file its last holder already removed.
limits: Older binaries take only the in-folder lock.
An unwritable parent directory disables the path lock.
Identity is by path: a symlinked spelling of the folder has its own lock, while the in-folder lock is still shared.
Crash safety between the two renames is unchanged.
The removed-file comparison is reasoned from POSIX unlink semantics; no test opens the file before another holder removes it.

items.title: Two first sign-ins at once no longer skip an address approval
items.summary: The app trusts the first address a device uses for a workspace and asks before trusting a different one. Which address was first is now settled in one step that two windows cannot both win.
items.before: Two windows signing in for the first time at once, through different addresses, were both trusted without asking. The second could open saved drafts and other local work carried over from the first address.
items.after: Exactly one first address is trusted on its own. The other window is told which address that was, and has to wait for the person's approval before it opens any saved work.
items.mechanism: Register the first trusted address with the storage owner's conditional initialize and decide admission from the record it returns, instead of a read followed by a separate write.

evidence.label: Two windows on one store, both reading nothing before either writes

limits: Approving a second address is still a read followed by a write. Two approvals at the same moment can leave one to be given again.
Where storage has no single step for this, the app falls back to the old read and write. The browser and the desktop app both have the single step.

technical.title: Make first trusted-address registration atomic
technical.summary: checkWorkspaceAddress initializes the trusted-address record through platform.storage.initialize and parses what comes back.
technical.before: An absent record led to storage.set of this window's address behind a per-Platform queue, so two windows that both read absence each admitted their own address.
technical.after: When the strict read finds nothing, the record is written with initialize, which stores only if nothing is stored and returns the stored value in one cross-window step. allowed is computed from the returned addresses, so the losing window sees the winner's address and is refused. Unreadable or malformed records still throw before anything is written.
limits: trustWorkspaceAddress remains a queued read plus set.
Platforms without initialize keep the read and set fallback.

items.title: A late reply no longer undoes a private notification setting
items.summary: When this window's own read or save of your notification setting crosses a change made in another window, the app now reads the saved setting again and shows that.
items.before: A late answer to an earlier read or save could overwrite a more private choice another window had just made. The saved setting stayed private, but this window went back to showing the full message in notifications.
items.after: If another window's change arrives while this window is waiting for an answer, neither is trusted to be the newer. The app reads what is saved now and uses that. Until the first read settles, notifications show nothing about messages.
items.mechanism: Track whether a request of this window's is out; a watch delivery during one marks the pair crossed, and the answer is replaced by a fresh strict read, repeated while crossings continue.

evidence.label: Held first reads and held saves crossed by another window's choice, in each order

limits: While the extra read is out after a crossed save, this window keeps showing what it showed before the save.
The saved setting underneath was already correct. This fixes what the window shows and uses.

technical.title: Fence stale notification preference replies
technical.summary: Own replies and watchRecord deliveries that overlap are resolved by an acknowledged current read.
technical.before: The initial get applied its reply unconditionally and watch deliveries before load were dropped; a mergeRecord reply was applied even when a newer watch value had already arrived.
technical.after: An asking flag covers the initial strict get and each save. A watch delivery while asking sets crossed instead of applying. current() loops a strict get until one completes uncrossed, then applies it or reports unreadable. A save applies its reply only if nothing crossed it, otherwise awaits current(); a failed save still reports its error. Watch deliveries while idle apply at once, as before.
limits: Ordering between two watch deliveries relies on the storage owner's delivery order.
The store is created through notificationPreviews(platform), exported for tests.

items.title: Enter no longer sends when its saved setting cannot be read
items.summary: If the app cannot read your saved Enter key setting, Enter now keeps starting a new line, and the settings say so and offer to try again.
items.before: The web version treated a setting it could not read as never set. Someone who chose to have Enter start a new line got the default instead, with no error shown, and Enter sent the message.
items.after: A setting that cannot be read, or that is not a real choice, leaves Enter as a new line. Composing settings show the problem with Try again, and choosing an option there replaces the unreadable one.
items.mechanism: Read the preference strictly and validate its shape; treat failure as unreadable with the safe default, and expose a retry.

evidence.label: A refused read and a malformed value in the real composer, and Try again in settings

limits: This only comes up when the device cannot read this one saved setting.
The message box itself shows no warning. The explanation is in Composing settings.

technical.title: Keep unreadable composer preferences visible and safe
technical.summary: useComposerPreferences reads with { strict: true } and rejects values that are not a boolean choice.
technical.before: A non-strict get mapped a refused read to null, which the store read as first use and set enterSends true.
technical.after: load() awaits a strict get, throws on a present value whose enterSends is not boolean, and on any failure sets enterSends false, unread true and the error text. retry re-runs load; setEnterSends clears unread on a successful write. Absent still means first use, with Enter sending.
limits: Applies to every platform adapter that honours strict reads.
No change to how Composer or ShortcutsDialog read enterSends.

items.title: A forgotten sign-in no longer comes back from another window
items.summary: Each change to the saved sign-ins is now made to the list as it is saved at that moment, not to the copy a window has had since it opened.
items.before: The app saved its whole list of sign-ins at once, as that window last knew it. A window that had been open a while could bring back a sign-in you removed in another window when it switched workspaces, or erase one another window had just saved.
items.after: A window reads the saved list, makes its one change and saves, in a single turn that other windows of the same browser wait for. Opening a sign-in that another window has since forgotten, or replaced with a newer one, does not put the old one back. A list that cannot be read is never saved over.
items.mechanism: Replace whole-list writes with queued read-change-write turns held under a Web Lock; make the open-workspace change conditional on the held sign-in still being stored.

evidence.label: A window left open while another forgets, adds or renews a sign-in, and a list that cannot be read

limits: A window left open still lists a sign-in another window forgot until it next changes something. Picking it opens the workspace for that visit, but does not save it again.

Browsers only let windows wait for each other on https pages and on this computer's own address. A workspace opened over plain http on a local network does without, so there two changes in the same instant can still lose one. The desktop app has one window and saves one change at a time.
Forgetting a sign-in removes it from this device. It does not sign that device out on the server.

technical.title: Merge saved sign-ins without reviving removals
technical.summary: App changes the stored servers list through serialized read-modify-write turns instead of writing its in-memory copy.
technical.before: persistServers(list) wrote the window's in-memory list as a whole, so a stale window's next workspace switch revived a forgotten sign-in or erased one stored by another window.
technical.after: changeServers(change) applies the change to memory at once, then in one turn does a strict get, applies the same change to the stored list and sets it, and replaces memory with what was stored. Turns queue per window and run under navigator.locks.request where available. Opening a workspace moves it to the front only if the sign-in was fresh or its url and token are still stored. Forget removes by url, sign-out by url and token, and the reset of all sign-ins runs in the same queue. A failed turn keeps its change for Retry.
limits: navigator.locks exists only in secure contexts (https, localhost, the desktop renderer); over plain http on a LAN the turn is not atomic across windows.
No watch: a stale window's displayed list is reconciled by its next turn.
Storage format and the desktop credential envelope are unchanged.

items.title: A canceled sign-in no longer opens its workspace
items.summary: Signing in with a saved sign-in, or setting the new password the host asked for, now ends when you cancel or leave.
items.before: After you canceled a saved sign-in or left the form and moved on, a late answer could still take you into the old workspace.
items.after: An answer that arrives after you cancel, choose another workspace or leave the screen is ignored. Signing in with a username and password already worked this way.
items.mechanism: Give the saved-token check the probe attempt counter and invalidate it on unmount; give the forced password replacement the auth card's attempt ticket.

evidence.label: A saved sign-in answered after Cancel and after the screen is gone; a replaced password saved late

limits: The request itself is not called off. Only what the app does with its answer changes.
The problem was in the screens, not in how the server checks sign-ins.

technical.title: End saved-sign-in and password attempts when canceled
technical.summary: openSaved and replacePassword complete only while their attempt is still the current one.
technical.before: openSaved called onConnected whenever me() resolved, and replacePassword whenever changePassword resolved, with no ownership check; cancelProbe bumped a counter only probe() read.
technical.after: openSaved takes a ticket from probeAttempt and returns early on a mismatch in both its success and failure paths; an unmount effect sets the counter to -1. replacePassword takes a ticket from the auth card's attempt ref, which its existing unmount cleanup already invalidates.
limits: No request is aborted; a late 401 after cancel no longer falls through to a probe.
The password sign-in submit path was already ticketed and is unchanged.

items.title: Open search results no longer keep deleted or edited text
items.summary: Search keeps its own copy of the results it found. It now asks for the same page again when a conversation in those results changes.
items.before: Text that was deleted, removed by automatic history removal, or edited stayed in a search that was already open until you searched again.
items.after: When a message is edited or deleted, history is removed, or you leave a conversation, an open search with results from that conversation asks the server for its page again, in place. This works even when that conversation's messages are not loaded.
items.mechanism: Record per conversation the seq of the latest content-changing event; the dialog re-requests its current page when that advances for a conversation among its results, never cutting a newer request short. Since UX-51 the results load more as they scroll, so the dialog reads them again from the top, in place, as far as they had been read.

evidence.label: A deleted result dropped, the same page asked again, a newer question left to finish
A real server's edit, deletion, pin and leave move the marker with no history loaded

limits: This is text the search had already shown. It never let anyone search for text they cannot see.
After being offline longer than the server keeps its record of changes, an open search is not refreshed until you search again.

technical.title: Keep open search results synchronized with content removal/edit
technical.summary: SearchDialog re-requests its current page when changedContent advances for a channel among its results.
technical.before: SearchDialog copied results into component state and nothing invalidated them; only loaded timelines reacted to message.updated, message.deleted or history.removed.
technical.after: WorkspaceState.changedContent maps a channel to the seq of its latest message.updated, message.deleted, pin event, history.removed or own member.left. The dialog compares the latest marker across its results' channels with the level captured when those results were requested, and re-runs the submitted criteria at the same cursor without scrolling. A request in flight is left to finish and its answer is checked against the level known when it was sent.
limits: The server remains the access filter; the client only asks again.
A full resync beyond the event log emits no per-message events, so it moves no marker.

items.title: A deleted message no longer stays in the Pinned panel
items.summary: The Pinned panel now asks again whenever anything already in its conversation changes, not only when the messages the app has loaded change.
items.before: A pinned message that was deleted stayed in an open Pinned panel when the app had not loaded that part of the conversation.
items.after: The panel follows every pin, unpin, edit and deletion in its conversation. It asks for the page it is on again, keeps what it shows until the answer arrives, and ignores answers to older requests.
items.mechanism: Pass the conversation's content-change marker to the shared list panel as a refresh key that re-requests the current page in place.

evidence.label: A deleted pin dropped with no history loaded, the list kept while asking, the same page asked again

limits: Any edit or deletion in the conversation makes the open panel ask again, pinned or not.
This is a message the app had already fetched. It gave no one access they did not have.

technical.title: Refresh Pins independently of loaded timeline state
technical.summary: PinsPanel refreshes on changedContent for its channel, in addition to the loaded timeline's pin signature.
technical.before: PinsPanel's reload key was derived from pinned messages in the loaded timeline, so a pin event or deletion for a message outside that window changed nothing.
technical.after: MessageListPanel takes an optional refreshKey. When it changes, the last requested page is requested again with the same cursor, without clearing the list or scrolling; the existing AbortController drops the older request's answer.
limits: The refresh is per conversation, not per pinned message.
Saved and Threads keep their existing reload keys.

items.title: Follow then Unfollow now ends unfollowed
items.summary: The app now sends its Follow and Unfollow requests for a thread one at a time, in the order you chose them.
items.before: If you clicked Follow then Unfollow, both requests went out together. The thread could end up followed when the older request reached the server last.
items.after: The second request waits until the first is answered, so the server ends on your latest choice. Marking a thread unread, which also follows it, waits its turn the same way. Reading a thread does not wait.
items.mechanism: Chain follow-changing requests per thread so each is sent after the previous one settles; leave forward-only thread reads unqueued; send nothing queued once the client is destroyed.

evidence.label: A slow Follow, a failed Follow and a closed client, against a real server

limits: A request that gets no answer holds back later Follow changes for that thread until the connection gives up on it.
Changes made on two of your devices at once are still settled by the server, not by this ordering.

technical.title: Order Follow/Unfollow by latest local intent
technical.summary: Follow-changing requests for one thread are serialized in the order they were made.
technical.before: setThreadFollow sent each request at once; a Follow overtaken on the way by the Unfollow after it left the thread followed.
technical.after: inFollowOrder chains setThreadFollow and markThreadUnread per root id, sending each when the previous one settles, accepted or not. markThreadRead stays unqueued because its cursor only moves forward. A queued request is rejected unsent once the client is destroyed, and that rejection triggers no rollback.
limits: Head-of-line blocking: these requests carry no timeout, as with the pin/save/snooze queue.
Cross-device ordering still relies on the server's revision.

items.title: A failed Mark unread no longer undoes one that worked
items.summary: The app now tells one Mark unread attempt from another, even when both are for the same message.
items.before: Marking the same message unread twice looked like one change. If the first attempt failed after the second had succeeded, the app undid the mark and showed the conversation as read, while the server still had it unread.
items.after: Only the latest attempt can undo the mark, and only if nothing has moved the reading position since. If every attempt fails, the position goes back to where it was before the first. If an earlier one worked and a later one fails, it goes back to the one that worked.
items.mechanism: Track the latest unanswered mark per conversation with the cursor it rolls back to; a superseded failure does nothing, and a success becomes the target a later failure returns to.

evidence.label: Repeated marks answered in each order: the older fails, both fail, the later fails

limits: With three or more attempts unanswered at once, the position it returns to can be one step out until the server next reports it.

technical.title: Identify unread rollback by request rather than cursor equality
technical.summary: Each Mark unread owns its rollback through a per-conversation record of the latest unanswered mark.
technical.before: The failure handler compared only the cursor value, so an older failure rolled back after a newer identical request had succeeded.
technical.after: unreadMarks keeps the seq and rollback cursor of the latest unanswered mark. A failure acts only while its mark is still the latest and the cursor is where it put it. A repeat made while the earlier mark still shows inherits that mark's rollback cursor; an earlier success moves a later mark's rollback cursor to the confirmed one.
limits: Rollback cursors are exact for two overlapping marks; longer overlapping chains settle on the next authoritative snapshot.

items.title: A closed profile no longer pulls you into a direct message
items.summary: Clicking Message on someone's profile now ends with the profile. Close it, and the click is dropped.
items.before: After you closed the profile and went to another channel, the old click still opened your direct message with that person.
items.after: Once the profile is closed, or shows someone else, a late answer opens nothing and changes nothing on the card.
items.mechanism: Count presses in a ref, invalidate the count on unmount or a change of person, and let only the current press navigate or set state.

evidence.label: A conversation that arrives after the card closed, and after it changed person

limits: The direct message may still be created on the server. Only the jump into it is dropped.

technical.title: Cancel Profile Message navigation ownership on dismissal
technical.summary: A Profile Message completion navigates only while its press is still the card's current one.
technical.before: The awaited openDm completion called onOpenDm after the dialog had unmounted.
technical.after: A press counter ref is bumped by each press and by the cleanup of an effect keyed on userId. Completion, error and busy state apply only while the counter still matches; a change of user also resets the busy and error state.
limits: openDm is not aborted, so the server may still create the conversation.

items.title: A failed invite setting no longer leaves a server running unseen
items.summary: When the desktop app starts hosting, the server accepts connections before the app applies the invite setting. If that step fails, the app now stops the server it just started.
items.before: If saving that setting failed, the app lost track of the server. Stopping hosting reported success, but the server still answered and the workspace folder stayed locked.
items.after: The app keeps hold of the new server until startup has fully worked. If a step fails, the server is stopped and the workspace is reported as not started, so it can be started again.
items.mechanism: Move the start adapter into its own module and run the setup that follows listening in a protected block, which stops the server and clears relay tracking before the failure is reported.

evidence.label: A real server whose database refuses the invite write, then starts once it takes it

limits: The test makes the database refuse the write on purpose. A real disk failure was not staged.
If the server also fails to stop, the app says so and asks to be reopened. It can do no more from there.

technical.title: Close a created listener when post-start invite setup fails
technical.summary: startHostedServer owns the server between its creation and its handover.
technical.before: The adapter inline in index.ts threw from setInviteOnly after createWorkspaceServer had resolved, dropping the only reference to a listening server that held its folder lock.
technical.after: The adapter lives in hostedServer.ts with its dependencies passed in. relayServers.add and setInviteOnly run in a try block whose catch deletes the relay entry and awaits server.stop() before rethrowing; a stop that fails too surfaces as an AggregateError of both errors.
limits: Real SQLite with a write-refusing trigger and a loopback listener establish the failure; the failed-stop branch uses a stub server.
N12's controller and connector cleanup is unchanged.

items.title: Quitting no longer waits without limit behind a stuck backup
items.summary: Quitting the desktop app waits in line behind a backup that is still running. That wait now has a time limit.
items.before: If a backup hung, quitting waited with no limit, because the timed part of stopping had not started yet. In a test, the server was still running after six times that limit, and the choice to keep the app open or quit anyway never came up.
items.after: After the limit, the app says it could not finish stopping and offers to keep it open or quit anyway. The backup carries on, the server stays under the app's control, and nothing stops later by surprise.
items.mechanism: Give the queued stop a deadline for reaching its turn, equal to the cleanup timeout. On expiry the turn is given up, so the queued operation does nothing when reached, and shutdown is rejected.

evidence.label: A quit behind a held backup gives up, stops nothing later, then stops on the next try

limits: The test held a backup open on purpose. It did not show a real backup stuck on a network drive.
The backup is not called off. Quitting anyway ends it, and the next backup clears away what it left.
The Stop hosting button still waits behind a running backup with no limit.

technical.title: Bound shutdown waiting before it reaches cleanup
technical.summary: shutdown() waits cleanupTimeoutMs for its turn in the operation queue, then abandons the turn.
technical.before: serialized(stopCurrent) joined the queue behind an outstanding backup with no deadline, so finishCleanup's timer never started.
technical.after: The queued stop and a timer share a three-state turn: waiting, taken, given up. The timer rejects shutdown and marks the turn given up, so the queued operation returns without stopping when it is finally reached. If the turn comes first, the timer is cleared and stopCurrent runs with its own deadlines. A rejection resets closing, as a failed stop does.
limits: A held adapter proves the queue behavior, not a real blocked network-share backup.
Preceding work is not cancelled; ownership of the worker and the server is unchanged.
stop() outside a quit is still unbounded behind queued work.
